title: Dwoje dzieci · dwaj studenci
title_en: Counting mixed groups, and the other way to count men
note: C1-SPINE Block 8 unit 3. Two facts, both about counting PEOPLE, which is the spine's stated reason for sharing a unit and why it sits after the whole virile apparatus. SEVEN NEW STRINGS AND NOT ONE NEW ENDING OR AGREEMENT RULE - that is what makes the double load legal here. (1) COLLECTIVE NUMERALS dwoje/troje/czworo/piecioro: for a group with both men and women in it, and for children. They pull the Genitive plural (owned - gen_pl, gen_pl_full, num_virile) and the neuter-singular verb (owned - num_subject taught exactly this for five-and-up), so the only new material is the four words. (2) DWAJ, which b2_num_virile [160] fenced by name with 'it is a second system - nominative numeral, nominative noun, plural verb - and would undo slide 2's entire claim in one line'. That claim (with the man-numbers there is no 2-4 exception) is now a level behind and safe to sit beside its alternative. DELIBERATE DEVIATION FROM THE SPINE'S LETTER, LOGGED: the spine says 'dwaj'; this unit teaches dwaj, trzej AND czterej. They are the COMPLETE closed set - there is no nominative virile numeral above four - and teaching one of three would leave the learner with a shape he cannot use for the other two numbers he meets constantly, which is the half-teaching this course avoids. Two extra strings, no extra mechanism. Slide 3 states plainly that the set stops at four and that from five up pieciu studentow jest is the only option. THE FEMININE GUARD IS CARRIED FORWARD FROM b2_num_virile, which called it 'the most important thing in the pack': osoba is FEMININE, so it takes the ordinary numbers - piec osob - and neither the man-numbers nor the collectives. Quiz item 8 and use item 10 are that guard. kobiet (the Genitive plural of kobieta) is NOT TAUGHT anywhere in the course and was wanted for a second guard example; it was refused and osob used instead, which is b2_num_virile's own example. NOT TAUGHT, deliberately: collective numerals with PLURAL-ONLY nouns (dwoje drzwi) - the same word in a third job, cheap but a third job, and drzwi/okulary/spodnie are the only owned members; the -oro set above piecioro, named as continuing but with no forms shown so nothing untagged reaches the screen; and dwiema/dwoma (the oblique numerals), which no unit needs. CAUGHT IN SELF-REVIEW AND REMOVED: a use item read 'Czterej koledzy graja w pilke' - pilke is TAUGHT (a2_sport [94], in 'Mam nowa pilke') but 'grac w pilke' is w + ACCUSATIVE, an untaught governor (prep_w_loc is w + Locative), and the phrase appears nowhere in the course. Replaced with 'Czterej koledzy pija kawe'. HOMOGRAPH WATCH: dzieci is TAUGHT (a2_family2 [58]) and its Genitive plural is the SAME STRING, so troje dzieci uses a form the learner already reads correctly - named on slide 1 rather than left to look like a new word.

intro.title: A third set of numbers — for mixed groups, and for children
intro.body:
You already have two sets of numbers for counting: the ordinary ones (dwa koty, pięć osób) and the man-numbers (dwóch studentów). There is a third, and it covers the case the other two cannot: a group with men and women in it, and children.

Dwoje, troje, czworo, pięcioro. Four words, and that is the whole of what is new here.

Everything they pull, you own. The noun goes into the many-form, exactly as it does after pięć. The verb goes into the -o form, exactly as it does after pięć. And dzieci is its own many-form already — the word looks the same after troje as it does on its own, so there is nothing extra to learn there either.

The set continues upward in the same shape past five, but these four cover the groups you will actually be counting.
intro.body_pl: Dwoje dzieci. Troje dzieci. Czworo dzieci. Pięcioro dzieci.

intro.title: Which set, and when
intro.title_pl: Dwa koty · dwóch studentów · dwoje studentów
intro.body:
The question is never what the words mean. It is what kind of word the noun is, and whether the group is mixed.

Things and animals take the ordinary numbers. Feminine words take the ordinary numbers too — and this is the one that catches people: osoba means person, but it is feminine, so it is pięć osób and never anything else. That was true when you learned the man-numbers and it is still true now.

Men only: the man-numbers. Men and women together, or children: the collectives.

So dwóch studentów is two male students, and dwoje studentów is one of each. Same noun, same number, different group — and the numeral is the only thing that says so.
intro.body_pl: Dwa koty. Pięć osób. Dwóch studentów. Dwoje studentów.

rows: two students (a man and a woman)

intro.title: Dwaj studenci są — the other way to count men
intro.title_pl: Dwóch studentów jest = dwaj studenci są
intro.body:
When you learned the man-numbers you learned one shape: dwóch studentów jest — numeral and noun in the many-form, verb in the singular.

There is a second shape, just as common, and it is the plain one. Dwaj studenci są. The numeral names, the noun names, and the verb is an ordinary plural. Nothing is pulled anywhere.

The two mean exactly the same thing. Choose either.

The catch is that this shape exists only for two, three and four — dwaj, trzej, czterej. There is no such word above four. From five up, pięciu studentów jest is your only option, and that is the shape you already have.
intro.body_pl: Dwaj studenci są. Trzej synowie są. Czterej koledzy są.

examples.en: Two students are in the park.

intro.title: Which numeral pulls which verb
intro.title_pl: Dwaj są · dwóch jest · dwoje jest
intro.body:
One table, and it settles every sentence in this unit.

Only the naming shapes take a plural verb. Everything that pulls the noun into the many-form pulls the verb into the singular as well — and in the past that singular is the -o form, which is the one you met with pięć.
intro.body_pl: Dwa koty są. Dwaj studenci są. Dwóch studentów jest. Dwoje dzieci jest.

examples.en: Four children were in the park.
Two students were in the shop.

match.en: two people — a man and a woman
two students — a man and a woman
two students — both men, naming shape
three students — all men, naming shape
four students — all men, naming shape

quiz.explain: Children take the collectives. Neither the ordinary numbers nor the man-numbers work here, whichever children they are.
The collectives run past five the same way they start. Troje is three.

quiz.prompt: two students — one man and one woman →
quiz.explain: The other two are both correct Polish for two MALE students. Only the collective says the group is mixed — and the noun is the same word in all three.
Dwaj is a naming shape, so nothing is pulled anywhere and the verb is an ordinary plural.
This is the shape you already had: the numeral pulls the noun into the many-form and the verb into the singular. Same meaning as dwaj studenci są, opposite machinery.
The collectives behave like pięć: singular verb now, the -o form in the past.
Trzej is the naming shape, so the noun names too — synowie, the plural you learned in the -owie family. Synów is the many-form that goes with trzech.
Osoba means person but it is a feminine word, so it takes the ordinary numbers and nothing else. This is the one that catches everybody.

quiz.prompt: two doctors — both men, naming shape →
quiz.explain: Lekarze is the naming plural, and dwaj is the numeral that leaves it alone. Dwoje lekarzy would be one man and one woman.
Czterej counts men in the naming shape and cannot reach children; czterech is the man-number. Only czworo does this job.

quiz.prompt: two people — a man and a woman →
quiz.explain: Dwóch ludzi is two men. Dwie osoby is two people with nothing said about who they are — correct, but it is not what the collective says.
The collective is the only one of the four that says the group is mixed.

type_items.explain: Dzieci is already its own many-form, so the noun does not move at all.

type_items.prompt_en: two people — a man and a woman
type_items.explain: Ludzi is the many-form of ludzie, and it is the form every one of these numerals pulls.

type_items.prompt_en: two students — both men, naming shape
type_items.explain: Naming numeral, naming noun. Nothing is pulled into the many-form here.

type_items.prompt_en: three students — all men, naming shape
four students — all men, naming shape
type_items.explain: Four is where this set stops. There is no word above it — five is pięciu studentów and the other machinery.
The -o verb after it is your clue: only a numeral that pulls the noun can pull było as well.

type_items.prompt_en: Two students are in the park.
type_items.explain: Dwaj leaves everything in its naming shape, so the verb is a plain plural.
Two children, and still the singular -o form — the collectives behave like pięć at every number.

use_items.prompt_en: Type: Two children are at home.
Type: Five children were at school.
Type: Two students are at school. (both men, naming shape)
Type: Two students are at school. (both men, the shape you already had)
use_items.explain: The same sentence twice over, in the two shapes Polish allows. Nothing chooses between them but your ear.

use_items.prompt_en: Type: Three sons live in Poland.
Type: Three children have a dog.
use_items.explain: Ma, not mają — the collective pulls the verb into the singular even when three people own the dog.

use_items.prompt_en: Type: Four children were in the park.
Type: Two doctors work in the hospital.
Type: Two students live in Poland. (a man and a woman)
use_items.explain: Mieszka, singular, because the collective pulls the verb the way pięć does.

use_items.prompt_en: Type: Five people were in the shop.
use_items.explain: Osoba is feminine, so it takes the ordinary numbers — not the collectives and not the man-numbers.

use_items.prompt_en: Type: Three people are waiting for the bus.
Type: Four friends are drinking coffee.
use_items.explain: Naming numeral, naming noun, plural verb — and the object behaves exactly as it always has.
